source_text: Commentariorum Series — Veteris interpretationis Origenis in Matthaeum. Post mandata dilectionis Dei et proximi quaeritur quomodo omnis lex et prophetae pendeant in duobus mandatis. Qui implevit dilectionem Dei et proximi dignus est sapientia et sermone scientiae per Spiritum, et exsultat in sapientia Dei.
thought_title: The Two Great Commandments as the Hinge of All Scripture
orientation: Origen is opening his treatment of the two great commandments, explaining how the whole law and prophets hang on love of God and neighbor.
pass_a_gloss: After the commandments of love of God and neighbor, it is asked how all the law and the prophets hang on the two commandments. The one who has fulfilled love of God and neighbor is worthy of wisdom and of the word of knowledge through the Spirit, and exults in the wisdom of God.

choices.why: The glossary does not fix this phrase, but 'love' is the standard rendering of dilectio in this context, and 'neighbor' is the plain sense of proximus.
The verb pendeo means to hang or depend; 'hang' preserves the physical metaphor of the biblical image of the law suspended on the commandments.
This is a Pauline phrase (1 Corinthians 12:8) rendered literally; 'word' keeps sermo as a single utterance or message, and 'knowledge' is the plain sense of scientia.

choices.english: exults in the wisdom of God
choices.why: Exsulto means to rejoice or exult; 'exults' conveys the active joy in God's wisdom, and 'wisdom of God' is the literal rendering.
rejected: rejoices in the wisdom of God

bible_refs.note: omnis lex et prophetae pendeant in duobus mandatis

pass_b_english: After the commandments to love God and neighbor, the question arises how the whole law and the prophets hang on these two commandments (Matthew 22:40). Whoever has fulfilled the love of God and neighbor is worthy of wisdom and the word of knowledge through the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:8), and exults in the wisdom of God.
